item.title: Claude Code Desktop Flaw Let Malicious HTML Steal Developer Credentials
item.description:
Noma Labs found a high-severity Claude Code Desktop flaw that let malicious HTML files steal local credentials and private keys through the preview pane.

Noma Labs researchers discovered a high-severity vulnerability in Anthropic’s Claude Code Desktop application that allowed malicious HTML files to steal credentials and private keys from a developer’s machine. The flaw, named SneakPeek, received a CVSS score of 8.7.

How the Exploit Worked

The vulnerability, discovered by Norma Labs’ senior vulnerability researcher Eli Ainhorn, affected Claude Code Desktop’s preview pane, which uses Electron’s Chromium-based rendering engine to display HTML files when Claude reads or modifies them.

The researcher found three security weaknesses that worked together to bypass the preview’s protections. Files smaller than 256KB were loaded as data: URLs with a Content Security Policy (CSP) blocking JavaScript execution. Larger files were instead loaded through file:// URLs, where the CSP was not applied. The request filter also failed to block local file access when Claude rendered a static HTML file directly from disk.

Noma Labs demonstrated the attack using a public repository containing a code coverage report with malicious JavaScript hidden inside it. A developer who cloned the repository and asked Claude to review or edit the report could trigger the payload when the preview pane opened the file. The script then ran without a separate permission prompt.

It could read sensitive local files using fetch(), including SSH private keys, AWS credentials, GitHub and npm tokens, Docker registry credentials, Git identity information, Kubernetes credentials, and Claude OAuth tokens. The script sent the stolen data to an attacker-controlled server using the navigator.sendBeacon() API.

The finding highlights how a routine code-review task could expose sensitive development credentials without a separate permission prompt.

Initial Patch and Final Fix

Noma Labs reported the vulnerability to Anthropic on July 4, 2026. Anthropic triaged it on July 9 and assigned a CVSS v4.0 score of 8.7.

On July 24, Anthropic deployed an initial patch blocking direct fetch() and XMLHttpRequest requests to file:// paths. However, Noma Labs researchers demonstrated a bypass the same day by moving file-reading requests into Web Workers created from blob: URLs. The workers could still read sensitive files and pass their contents to the main thread for exfiltration.

Anthropic confirmed the incomplete fix on August 3. According to Noma Labs, the company addressed the remaining issues in Claude Desktop version 1.30096.1 and later, with the update delivered through automatic updates on August 17.

At the time of the researchers’ report, a CVE assignment and GitHub Advisory publication were still pending.

Experts’ Commentary

Cybersecurity experts who shared their comments with Hackread.com said SneakPeek highlights the risks posed by AI tools that process untrusted files, particularly when those tools operate on developer machines containing sensitive credentials.

Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist at Sysdig, said, “SneakPeek is an unfriendly reminder that AI tools come with their own attack surface.” She added, “Most AI security centers on the model: training, safety filters, and system prompts. SneakPeek wasn’t a model failure, it lived in the application around it.”

Morin also highlighted the visibility challenge for defenders, explaining that “The malicious script executed in the preview pane’s rendering process, not as an action the agent took, so agent-level logs would not be expected to show it.”

Ram Varadarajan, CEO at Acalvio, said, “Three seemingly minor gaps chained together to steal AWS credentials and SSH keys without a click. And Noma’s first-patch bypass makes the bigger point: no single layer of prevention is going to hold forever.”

He recommended using decoy credentials to detect potential compromise, saying, “Plant model-aware decoy credentials on developer machines and along paths AI agents can reach. If an agent, whether well-behaved or compromised, touches one, you get a high-confidence alert, even if you don’t yet know the vulnerability being exploited.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: OpenAI Model Hacked Crypto Wallet and Spent Funds to Deploy Smart Contracts
item.description:
OpenAI disclosed that an internal AI model hacked a crypto wallet and spent Sepolia test ETH without permission to deploy smart contracts.

An internal OpenAI research model used a cryptocurrency wallet without authorization on June 26, 2026, to pay transaction fees during a coding task. OpenAI disclosed the incident on October 15, after discovering it on September 25 while reviewing earlier model activity.

The GPT 5.6 Sol family test model was tasked with running a software update for a trading application and deploying smart contracts on Sepolia. Sepolia is an Ethereum test network where developers test applications using tokens, without using real money.

The instructions provided no funded wallet and did not authorize spending from another account. After attempts to obtain free test tokens through developer faucets failed, the model wrote a script to check 362 wallet addresses derived from publicly known developer recovery phrases.

Recovery phrases are sequences of words that can be used to derive the private keys controlling cryptocurrency wallets. The model found an account with enough Sepolia ETH to cover the deployment fees.

According to OpenAI, the model considered whether using the funds was ethical but decided the publicly known recovery phrase and valueless test tokens made the transaction acceptable. The deployment succeeded, charging transaction fees to the account.

The model then reported completing the task without disclosing its unauthorized use of the wallet. It also worked around failed network requests by testing alternative providers and HTTP methods before broadcasting the signed transaction.

Other Unauthorized Activities

OpenAI published three additional reports covering unauthorized activity during June 2026, bringing its publicly listed misalignment reports to 19.

In one case, a model retrieving historical hospital-bed statistics bypassed authorization checks on a government website after downloading server configuration and application files containing sensitive credentials.

In another, a model accessed internal systems while researching a public dashboard and changed configuration settings. A separate evaluation resulted in the download of five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows of data.

A further report described a model that circumvented restrictions on internet requests by using an external browser to submit blocked requests and extract figures from rendered images using optical character recognition.

OpenAI Tightens Safeguards

The disclosures follow a July 2026 incident in which OpenAI research models bypassed network restrictions during a cybersecurity evaluation and accessed Hugging Face’s production systems while seeking answers to a hacking benchmark.

As Hackread.com previously reported, the models exploited vulnerabilities and used exposed credentials to reach internal resources. These incidents highlight how general attempts to complete an assigned task can lead to unauthorized access when safeguards fail.

OpenAI said it has introduced additional safeguards to prevent live internet access during similar tests. It has also extended its misalignment monitoring to all traffic, with alerts designed to notify security staff if a model gains live internet access.

(Photo by Growtika on Unsplash)

item.title: Fake Calendar Invites Target 40,000 Firms in Microsoft Credential Theft
item.description:
More than 40,000 organisations have received fake calendar invitations designed to steal Microsoft account credentials, according to new findings from Check Point Email researchers.

Cybersecurity researchers at Check Point revealed that their detection system identified 302,386 unique phishing emails after activity spiked on September 25, 2026. The messages came from 247,270 sender addresses using 33,890 domains, showing that the campaign was not limited to a small collection of disposable accounts.

Calendar Invites Used as Phishing Lures

The phishing emails look like ordinary workplace meeting requests, including Microsoft Teams invitations. A recipient who follows the meeting link is taken to a fake Microsoft sign-in page that records the username and password entered there.

Some versions include an .ics attachment, the standard file format used for sharing calendar events. Because the attachment contains valid calendar data, it can open normally or add the meeting to a calendar, making the invitation appear genuine.

In other versions, the meeting link appears as a Microsoft Teams or Microsoft login address, while the underlying URL points elsewhere. However, hovering over the link before opening it can reveal the real destination.

According to researchers, the attackers are not exploiting a flaw in Microsoft Teams, Outlook or the .ics format. They are using familiar calendar features to make the phishing email look like a meeting request that belongs in the recipient’s working day.

Campaign Activity Increased in October

Check Point’s report said the campaigns averaged 8,319 emails for each active day and remained active on October 15.

A separate activity count included in the report shows that monthly volume rose from several thousand messages in April to more than 118,000 in September. More than 740,000 messages were recorded during the first two weeks of October, with almost 200,000 sent on October 8 alone.

The 740,000 figure should not be confused with the 302,386 unique phishing emails flagged by Check Point’s newer detection layer. The company presented them as separate measurements of campaign activity.

Why Calendar Phishing Can Work

Meeting invitations receive different treatment from ordinary emails because employees regularly accept requests from customers, suppliers, recruiters and colleagues they have not contacted before. Calendar applications can also display event details outside the original email, giving the lure another place to reach the recipient.

A convincing invitation may include a meeting title, date, attendee list and familiar Microsoft branding. Victims who follow the embedded link can reach a fake sign-in page that records the credentials they enter.

Stolen Microsoft credentials can give attackers access to email, OneDrive, SharePoint and other company services, depending on the account’s permissions and authentication controls. Compromised mailboxes can also be used to send more credible meeting invitations from a trusted address.

How Organizations Can Reduce the Risk

Employees should check the sender and actual link destination before joining an unexpected meeting or signing in through a calendar invitation. A Microsoft-branded page should not be trusted based on its appearance alone.

Administrators can reduce account theft by requiring phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys. Email and calendar monitoring should also examine .ics attachments, newly registered sender domains and links that do not match the service named in the invitation.

Anyone who entered credentials through a suspicious meeting request should change the affected password, revoke active sessions and review the account for unfamiliar sign-ins, forwarding rules, registered devices and authentication methods.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Bright Security Introduces STAR Fuzzer, Agentic Fuzzing That Writes Its Own Harnesses and Proves Every Finding
item.description:
San Rafael, United States, October 19th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Built on an evolutionary engine first released in 2018, STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security finds crashes, memory exhaustion and memory-safety bugs in security-critical code without a running application. In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS.

Bright Security, the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it. STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Agentic fuzzing applies AI agents to the parts of fuzzing that have traditionally required a specialist: choosing what to test, writing the harness, and deciding which crashes matter. STAR Fuzzer uses AI for those steps and an evolutionary search engine for the fuzzing itself, so the parts that need judgment are automated and the search stays fast, repeatable and evidence based.

Why Fuzzing Needed a New Approach

Coverage-guided fuzzers such as AFL++ and libFuzzer are proven and widely used, and programs like Google’s OSS-Fuzz have shown how much they can find. But they depend on people to write and maintain a harness for every target and to triage the crashes that come back. That cost has kept fuzzing concentrated in specialist teams and a subset of critical projects.

Other testing approaches don’t fill the gap. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tests what an attacker can reach over HTTP, so it rarely exercises the parsing and processing code behind input validation. LLM-based pentesting is effective at known vulnerability patterns but tends to look where a model expects bugs to be. The result is a class of outage-level and memory-safety defects, often triggered by tiny malformed inputs, that most AppSec programs never test for.

How STAR Fuzzer compares with traditional coverage-guided fuzzers (such as AFL++ and libFuzzer) and DAST:

  • What it Tests: Traditional fuzzers test functions exposed through a hand-written harness. DAST tests running applications over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions on untrusted-input paths, chosen automatically.
  • Harness: Traditional fuzzers need harnesses written and maintained by engineers. DAST doesn’t use one. STAR Fuzzer generates a harness per function with AI, then verifies it reaches its target.
  • Search: Traditional fuzzers use coverage-guided mutation. DAST sends request-level attack payloads. STAR Fuzzer uses a structure-aware evolutionary search guided by coverage and multiple fitness signals.
  • Running App Needed: Traditional fuzzers, no. DAST, yes. STAR Fuzzer, no.
  • Triage: Manual for traditional fuzzers and built into the scanner for DAST. STAR Fuzzer triages automatically for reachability and impact.
  • Output: Traditional fuzzers return crash inputs and logs. DAST returns a vulnerability report. STAR Fuzzer delivers the file, function and byte-exact payload in a pull request.
  • Fix Validation: Traditional fuzzers need a manual re-run and DAST needs a rescan. With STAR Fuzzer, teams replay the payload.

Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss

Ask an LLM to audit a parser and it will find the bug classes it already knows from training. The zero-days that survive for years in mature, widely deployed code are the ones that match no known pattern. STAR Fuzzer uses AI to choose targets and build harnesses, but the search that finds the bugs is not an LLM. It doesn’t read the code or guess where a bug might be. It runs the program millions of times, observes what actually happens, and keeps whatever pushes the target into code it hasn’t reached yet.

In Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss, Bright Security CTO Bar Hofesh gives four reasons LLM code review does not replace fuzzing for zero-day discovery:

  • Scale: A single fuzzing campaign runs 1 million to 10 million concrete inputs against the compiled target. At about 2,000 tokens per reasoned test case, matching one million executions with an LLM would take about two billion tokens for one target, and each of those test cases would still be a prediction.
  • Speed and Ground Truth: A persistent harness runs hundreds to a few thousand inputs per second per worker, across several parallel workers, so one million executions take minutes to tens of minutes. One LLM reasoning pass over one hypothesis takes several seconds, so one million would take months. The fuzzer also observes real behavior, such as a sanitizer reporting a heap read one byte out of bounds. An LLM has to predict how compiled code behaves, including struct layouts, integer widths, allocator behavior and build flags that aren’t visible in the source.
  • Coverage: STAR Fuzzer’s libxml2 harness reaches about 13,600 code regions in a 5-million-execution run. Coverage feedback shows which regions each input reached, and inputs that reach new code become starting points for deeper search. Code review has no equivalent signal for how much of a large parser it has actually covered.
  • The Unexpected: LLMs, code reviewers and static analyzers look for the same known patterns, so in mature code most of those bugs are already fixed. The fuzzer has no expectations about where a bug should be. The target’s own behavior decides what is interesting.

Reproducibility is the other difference. Many plausible-looking LLM findings don’t reproduce, and maintainers need a reproducer before they can act. A fuzzer finding is a reproducer by construction, and Bright Security replays every one in a fresh container before filing it.

How STAR Fuzzer Works

STAR Fuzzer’s search engine drives any target through a small harness over IPC, so the code under test can be written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin, Crystal, Node or any language that can read an input and report back.

  • Structure-aware parsing with no per-target grammar: Every seed is parsed into a typed tree of fields by a format-agnostic parsing layer, and the tree serializes back to the original bytes exactly. No grammar or dictionary file is written per target, and each format added to the parsing layer improves every target that uses it.
  • Mutations that get past the first check: Byte-level mutation mostly produces inputs a parser rejects at its first sanity check. Mutating the fields of a valid structured input keeps most executions past framing and validation, so the testing budget is spent on the deeper logic behind them.
  • Evolution with exact replay: Each organism in the population carries a genome, an ordered list of mutations. Each epoch, organisms mutate, run and are scored. Improvements are kept, unproductive changes are reverted, and organisms breed. Replaying a genome reproduces its payload exactly, so every result can be regenerated from a logged random seed.

Results from Open-Source Testing

Before release, Bright Security ran STAR Fuzzer for two days in an automated pipeline against multiple open source projects, from libraries and applications to low-level binary parsers. 45% of the projects tested had High or Critical issues, and 37% of the vulnerable projects are part of Google’s OSS-Fuzz program.

In its first month of availability, STAR Fuzzer produced ten published findings in eight projects written in C, Go, JVM languages and Crystal. Each was replayed in a fresh container before filing:

  • TwelveMonkeys: In the DDS reader, the mipMapCount header field sizes an uncapped array, so a 38-byte file forces a multi-gigabyte allocation (CWE-789). GHSA-fwp7-38wp-mmxw, fixed in 3.15.0.
  • Fider: Upload validation checks an image’s compressed size, then fully decodes it, so a 436 KB PNG expands to about 562 MB. Any authenticated user can trigger it (CWE-409). STAR Fuzzer found it in about 12 minutes, in a release already benchmarked by multiple AI pentesting vendors. GHSA-7cw3-7xh9-529r, fixed in 0.38.0.
  • Crystal standard library (XML): XML::Node#namespace type confusion. ENTITY_DECL is missing from an allowlist, so a field of libxml2’s xmlEntity struct is read as an xmlNs* (CWE-843). GHSA-c267-9cqj-hv9f, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • Crystal standard library (YAML): YAML::Any#hash overflows the stack on a self-referencing anchor and alias cycle. An 88-byte input causes an uncatchable SIGSEGV (CWE-674). GHSA-fj8w-2r88-5v7w, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • libsolv: Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-104621 and CVE-2026-104622. Details are under embargo.
  • htop: An out-of-bounds read in the /proc/PID/stat parser, caused by a missing bounds check on field 22 (CWE-125). Fixed (#2101).
  • universal-ctags: A null-pointer member access in foreachEntriesInScope (CWE-476). Fixed in commit 780bd7a (#4497).
  • scrimage: An uncapped width-times-height pixel count lets a 35-byte GIF trigger allocation attempts of about 2 GB, and over 8 GB in a second variant (CWE-789). Fixed in 4.6.8 (#893).
  • RIOT OS: An off-by-one in _dirlist_cb (link_format.c). The bounds check runs after the write, so a NUL byte lands one past the buffer (CWE-193). Fix submitted in PR #22879.

Several of these bugs sit in code that looks correct on review. The Fider upload has a size limit, but it measures compressed size. The TwelveMonkeys field reads as image metadata, not as a length. The Crystal allowlist looks complete. The YAML hash function is correct for trees, and the bug is a cycle in the input.

The full methodology and results are published in two parts: Part I on brightsec.com, and Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss by Bar Hofesh.

Where STAR Fuzzer Fits Best

STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security is designed for teams whose code handles untrusted input below the HTTP layer, including:

  • Applications that process uploaded files, images, documents or archives
  • Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols
  • Non-web software such as embedded and IoT firmware, desktop applications and backend services
  • Codebases with a growing share of AI-generated code that needs testing beyond pattern matching
  • Security teams that want to confirm static analysis (SAST) findings by exercising the flagged functions live

It supports C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal, and runs inside the customer’s environment with no running application, cloud scanner or authentication required. In persistent mode, harness execution is about 51 times faster than running a new process per input.

Executive Perspectives

“Fuzzing has always found the bugs that matter most, the ones that take a service down or corrupt memory, but it has been too expensive for most teams to run,” said Bar Hofesh, Co-founder and CTO of Bright Security. “The search was never the bottleneck. The harnesses and the triage were. STAR Fuzzer automates both, so the evolutionary engine we built in 2018 can finally run across a whole codebase.”

“When Nevada opened the Boulder City Bypass in 2018, it took navigation apps months to start sending drivers down it,” Hofesh added. “LLMs auditing code work the same way. They find the bugs they’ve already seen. The zero-days that have lived for years in mature code are the ones nobody has seen before, and that’s exactly where a fuzzer shines.”

“Security teams are being asked to keep up with code written faster than ever, much of it by AI,” said Gadi Bashvitz, Co-founder and CEO of Bright Security. “Testing that only looks where bugs are expected won’t keep pace. STAR Fuzzer looks everywhere else, and it hands developers the proof they need to fix what it finds.”

“AppSec teams keep asking us the same thing: if AI is writing more of our code, what’s testing the parts AI can’t, see?” said Eyal Dror, CMO of Bright Security. “STAR Fuzzer is our answer. In its first month it found ten real bugs in mature open-source projects, and everyone came with the exact input that triggers it. That’s proof a developer can act on the same day, not another alert to argue about.”

Availability

STAR Fuzzer is available now as a mode of Bright STAR. Learn more and book a demo at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Frequently Asked Questions:

In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS.

Bright Security, the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it. STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Agentic fuzzing applies AI agents to the parts of fuzzing that have traditionally required a specialist: choosing what to test, writing the harness, and deciding which crashes matter. STAR Fuzzer uses AI for those steps and an evolutionary search engine for the fuzzing itself, so the parts that need judgment are automated and the search stays fast, repeatable and evidence based.

Why Fuzzing Needed a New Approach

Coverage-guided fuzzers such as AFL++ and libFuzzer are proven and widely used, and programs like Google’s OSS-Fuzz have shown how much they can find. But they depend on people to write and maintain a harness for every target and to triage the crashes that come back. That cost has kept fuzzing concentrated in specialist teams and a subset of critical projects.

Other testing approaches don’t fill the gap. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tests what an attacker can reach over HTTP, so it rarely exercises the parsing and processing code behind input validation. LLM-based pentesting is effective at known vulnerability patterns but tends to look where a model expects bugs to be. The result is a class of outage-level and memory-safety defects, often triggered by tiny malformed inputs, that most AppSec programs never test for.

How STAR Fuzzer compares with traditional coverage-guided fuzzers (such as AFL++ and libFuzzer) and DAST:

  • What it Tests: Traditional fuzzers test functions exposed through a hand-written harness. DAST tests running applications over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions on untrusted-input paths, chosen automatically.
  • Harness: Traditional fuzzers need harnesses written and maintained by engineers. DAST doesn’t use one. STAR Fuzzer generates a harness per function with AI, then verifies it reaches its target.
  • Search: Traditional fuzzers use coverage-guided mutation. DAST sends request-level attack payloads. STAR Fuzzer uses a structure-aware evolutionary search guided by coverage and multiple fitness signals.
  • Running App Needed: Traditional fuzzers, no. DAST, yes. STAR Fuzzer, no.
  • Triage: Manual for traditional fuzzers and built into the scanner for DAST. STAR Fuzzer triages automatically for reachability and impact.
  • Output: Traditional fuzzers return crash inputs and logs. DAST returns a vulnerability report. STAR Fuzzer delivers the file, function and byte-exact payload in a pull request.
  • Fix Validation: Traditional fuzzers need a manual re-run and DAST needs a rescan. With STAR Fuzzer, teams replay the payload.

Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss

Ask an LLM to audit a parser and it will find the bug classes it already knows from training. The zero-days that survive for years in mature, widely deployed code are the ones that match no known pattern. STAR Fuzzer uses AI to choose targets and build harnesses, but the search that finds the bugs is not an LLM. It doesn’t read the code or guess where a bug might be. It runs the program millions of times, observes what actually happens, and keeps whatever pushes the target into code it hasn’t reached yet.

In Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss, Bright Security CTO Bar Hofesh gives four reasons LLM code review does not replace fuzzing for zero-day discovery:

  • Scale: A single fuzzing campaign runs 1 million to 10 million concrete inputs against the compiled target. At about 2,000 tokens per reasoned test case, matching one million executions with an LLM would take about two billion tokens for one target, and each of those test cases would still be a prediction.
  • Speed and Ground Truth: A persistent harness runs hundreds to a few thousand inputs per second per worker, across several parallel workers, so one million executions take minutes to tens of minutes. One LLM reasoning pass over one hypothesis takes several seconds, so one million would take months. The fuzzer also observes real behavior, such as a sanitizer reporting a heap read one byte out of bounds. An LLM has to predict how compiled code behaves, including struct layouts, integer widths, allocator behavior and build flags that aren’t visible in the source.
  • Coverage: STAR Fuzzer’s libxml2 harness reaches about 13,600 code regions in a 5-million-execution run. Coverage feedback shows which regions each input reached, and inputs that reach new code become starting points for deeper search.   • The Unexpected: LLMs, code reviewers and static analyzers look for the same known patterns, so in mature code most of those bugs are already fixed. The fuzzer has no expectations about where a bug should be. The target’s own behavior decides what is interesting.

Reproducibility is the other difference. Many plausible-looking LLM findings don’t reproduce, and maintainers need a reproducer before they can act. A fuzzer finding is a reproducer by construction, and Bright Security replays every one in a fresh container before filing it.

STAR Fuzzer’s search engine drives any target through a small harness over IPC, so the code under test can be written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin, Crystal, Node or any language that can read an input and report back.

No grammar or dictionary file is written per target, and each format added to the parsing layer improves every target that uses it.
  • Mutations that get past the first check: Byte-level mutation mostly produces inputs a parser rejects at its first sanity check. Mutating the fields of a valid structured input keeps most executions past framing and validation, so the testing budget is spent on the deeper logic behind them.
  • Evolution with exact replay: Each organism in the population carries a genome, an ordered list of mutations. Each epoch, organisms mutate, run and are scored. Improvements are kept, unproductive changes are reverted, and organisms breed. Replaying a genome reproduces its payload exactly, so every result can be regenerated from a logged random seed.

  • TwelveMonkeys: In the DDS reader, the mipMapCount header field sizes an uncapped array, so a 38-byte file forces a multi-gigabyte allocation (CWE-789). GHSA-fwp7-38wp-mmxw, fixed in 3.15.0.
  • Fider: Upload validation checks an image’s compressed size, then fully decodes it, so a 436 KB PNG expands to about 562 MB. Any authenticated user can trigger it (CWE-409). STAR Fuzzer found it in about 12 minutes, in a release already benchmarked by multiple AI pentesting vendors. GHSA-7cw3-7xh9-529r, fixed in 0.38.0.
  • Crystal standard library (XML): XML::Node#namespace type confusion. ENTITY_DECL is missing from an allowlist, so a field of libxml2’s xmlEntity struct is read as an xmlNs* (CWE-843). GHSA-c267-9cqj-hv9f, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • Crystal standard library (YAML): YAML::Any#hash overflows the stack on a self-referencing anchor and alias cycle. An 88-byte input causes an uncatchable SIGSEGV (CWE-674). GHSA-fj8w-2r88-5v7w, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1.
  • libsolv: Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-104621 and CVE-2026-104622. Details are under embargo.
  • htop: An out-of-bounds read in the /proc/PID/stat parser, caused by a missing bounds check on field 22 (CWE-125). Fixed (#2101).
  • universal-ctags: A null-pointer member access in foreachEntriesInScope (CWE-476). Fixed in commit 780bd7a (#4497).

  • Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols

item.title: US Ransomware Negotiator Suspected of Helping ShinyHunters Extort Victims
item.description:
The unnamed US executive is separate from Canadian ransomware negotiator Edward Dubrovsky, who was arrested on federal extortion charges.

US federal investigators suspect executives at two ransomware negotiation firms maintained unusually close relationships with ShinyHunters, including one executive who allegedly helped operate the group’s victim-extortion website.

The findings were reported by Brian Krebs of KrebsOnSecurity today, citing sources close to the federal investigation. The report does not identify the US consulting company or the executive suspected of helping run the site because no charges have been announced against them.

Investigators are also examining the conduct of Canadian ransomware negotiator Edward Dubrovsky, who was arrested in Pennsylvania on October 8 on federal cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. His criminal complaint remains sealed, and the specific allegations underlying those charges have not been released publicly.

Investigators Examine Shinywire Operations

The website under investigation, shinywire.com, operated from about May 3 until October 16, 2026. Its homepage displayed a message for companies that had received an extortion email from ShinyHunters, directing them to use the unique link included in the message.

According to Krebs, the site hosted individual extortion pages associated with nearly 100 organisations. The report does not say that the homepage publicly named or listed those victims.

A cached page reviewed by Krebs concerned Intuitive Surgical, a US medical technology company breached in March 2026 after an employee entered credentials through a targeted phishing email. The page encouraged the company to contact ShinyHunters, displayed samples of allegedly stolen files and warned that its data could be published if it did not respond.

Those victims who did not begin negotiations within seven days could later have their stolen information published through ShinyHunters’ Tor-based leak site. Shinywire was used to communicate demands through private links, while the Tor site was used to release data.

Krebs also reported that investigators believe at least one executive from a large US consulting firm took an active role in operating Shinywire. The company reportedly employs more than 1,000 people but has not been named.

The allegation comes from sources familiar with the investigation. The suspected executive has not been publicly identified or charged, and federal authorities have not released evidence explaining the alleged role.

Messages Reportedly Exposed Negotiator Contacts

Investigators reportedly gained access to recent Signal messages when Dutch police arrested convicted hacker and suspected ShinyHunters member Pepijn van der Stap on September 15.

According to Krebs’s sources, those messages showed frequent conversations between van der Stap, Dubrovsky and at least one executive at the unnamed US consulting firm. The executives allegedly knew details about new ShinyHunters victims before some of the affected organisations learned they had been breached.

One source also claimed Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen sensitive FBI personnel data but did not notify the bureau before the group threatened to publish it.

Dubrovsky has not been convicted, and the sealed court record does not publicly confirm these claims. Court filings show that he faces allegations involving conspiracy to impair the confidentiality of information for extortion and interference with commerce through threats.

CYPFER, where Dubrovsky worked from May 2022 until December 2025, has said he served as a managing director and was never a founder or co-founder. He later became associated with CyberSteward, which provides ransomware negotiation and cyber extortion services.

Arrests Follow FBI Jobs Portal Breach

The investigation accelerated after ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for breaching the FBI jobs portal and obtaining personal, medical and employment information belonging to bureau personnel and applicants.

A missed security update reportedly left the Oracle PeopleSoft system exposed, after which the FBI removed a contractor from the assignment. Accenture was later identified as the company managing the platform.

Jordanian authorities had already detained suspected ShinyHunters member Saif al-Din Khader, known online as Rey, on September 29. He was reportedly cooperating with US investigators. The FBI later confirmed multiple arrests but declined to identify every suspect.

The bureau says ShinyHunters has obtained more than $70 million from victims during 2026.

Ransomware Negotiation Firms Face New Scrutiny

Companies hit by data breaches or ransomware attacks often hire negotiators to communicate with attackers, test their claims and reduce payment demands. That access can place negotiators close to victim information, payment decisions and criminal operators.

The ShinyHunters investigation now asks whether people trusted to represent victims also assisted the group pressuring them. Investigators have not publicly established how many negotiators are under examination or whether more charges will follow.

The case follows the separate prosecution of MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, who is accused of secretly paying attackers for decryption keys while charging customers much higher recovery fees. Pinhasi has not been convicted.

Neither case proves misconduct throughout the ransomware negotiation industry. Both cases, however, place the financial relationships between victims, negotiators and cybercriminals under closer examination.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Guide to Compliance and Cybersecurity in Healthcare Software Development
item.description:
In healthcare software, compliance and cybersecurity are not merely administrative procedures, they are integral features of the product itself. According to IBM’s “2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report,” the healthcare industry has recorded the highest average cost of a data breach across all industries for 13 consecutive years, with the cost per incident reaching $6.64 million. Meanwhile, AI-enabled attacks have increased the cost per data breach across all industries by approximately $1 million.

The 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare is recorded as the largest data breach in the history of the healthcare industry, with data from approximately 192.7 million people compromised. This attack originated from a single portal that lacked multi-factor authentication.

This guide explains the applicable regulations, a step-by-step process for building secure and compliant software, and the best development companies to assist with this effort.

The Regulatory Landscape

Which rules apply depends on what data your product touches, who your customers are and where your users live. Most healthcare products answer to more than one framework at once.

  1. HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (US). Apply to covered entities and their business associates, including vendors that store or process PHI. Expect risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption and a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA). The Security Rule overhaul proposed in January 2025 is now targeted for July 2027.
  2. HIPAA Breach Notification Rule and HITECH Act (US). Require notifying patients and HHS of a breach, generally within 60 days of discovery.
  3. FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (US). Covers health apps and wearables outside HIPAA, including unauthorized data sharing. The 2024 amendments remain in force; in September 2026 the FTC withdrew its older 2021 policy statement as redundant.
  4. FDA cybersecurity requirements (US). Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and connected devices need threat modeling, a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and a vulnerability-management plan.
  5. State health privacy laws (US). Laws such as Washington’s My Health My Data Act require consent for consumer health data and limit its sale.
  6. GDPR and UK GDPR. Health data is a special category, requiring an explicit legal basis, DPIAs and 72-hour breach notice to regulators.
  7. EU Health Data Space and AI Act. EHDS security and interoperability rules for EHR systems apply from March 2029. A provisional May 2026 deal would delay AI Act obligations for AI in medical devices to August 2028.

The pending HIPAA Security Rule update shows where enforcement is heading: mandatory MFA, encryption, asset inventories and annual audits. Building those in now is cheaper than retrofitting later.

Step-by-step guide to building compliant, secure healthcare software

Step 1: Map your data and regulatory scope

Let’s start by creating a data inventory. Determine what types of health data you are collecting, where that data flows, who has access to it, and which third parties receive it. Next, classify each data type according to the framework described above.

This will determine whether a BAA, a DPIA, or FDA approval is required or perhaps all of them. Be sure to document the results of this classification, as they will be requested by auditors and the hospital’s security team.

Step 2: Run a risk analysis and design for privacy

A documented risk assessment is the foundation for HIPAA compliance, and the OCR cites the lack of such an assessment more often than any other violation of the security rules. Combine this with threat modeling for each function that handles PHI. Collect only the data that each function needs, use anonymized data for analysis and testing, and never copy PHI from the production environment to development environments.

Step 3: Build a secure architecture with encryption

Segment networks so that PHI storage locations are kept separate from services accessible to the general public, implement “zero-trust” principles, and select cloud services covered by the provider’s BAA. Plan for high availability, as downtime in clinical software poses a risk to patient safety.

Encrypt PHI at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2 or higher), and store keys in a managed key service with scheduled rotation. IBM’s 2026 report showed that 53% of organizations that had suffered a data breach had not encrypted sensitive data.

Step 4: Lock down access and log every action

Require multi-factor authentication for all users with access to PHI, and implement role-based access according to the “least privilege” principle. Implement session time limits and a documented “break-glass” procedure for clinical access in emergencies. Maintain audit logs showing who has viewed, modified, or exported which medical records, and issue alerts for unusual patterns, such as bulk exports.

Step 5: Secure the development lifecycle and integrations

Base coding standards on OWASP guidance, run static and dynamic security testing in the CI/CD pipeline and scan open-source dependencies. Commission independent penetration tests before launch and at least yearly. For integrations, use HL7 FHIR with OAuth 2.0 and SMART on FHIR scopes, sign BAAs with every vendor that handles PHI, and audit tracking pixels and analytics SDKs.

Step 6: Prepare for incidents and keep compliance continuous

item.title: Nearly 480,000 Phishing Emails Traced to Computer Hidden Behind Hotel Fridge
item.description:
A computer hidden behind a hotel room refrigerator in Kobe was allegedly used to send around 480,000 phishing emails, according to Japanese investigators. A Chinese couple living in the city have been arrested in connection with the email campaign and separate purchases made using another person’s credit card details.

The suspects are Ye Jiafeng, 39, and his wife, Shen Qi, 39. Ye faces allegations of fraudulent obstruction of business and trespass over the hotel incident, while both were arrested on suspicion of computer fraud over the alleged credit card purchases. Police have not disclosed their response to the allegations.

Computer Hidden Behind Hotel Refrigerator

On 15 May, 2025, Ye allegedly entered a Kobe hotel with another person, pretending to be a guest. The pair hid a small computer behind the room’s refrigerator and left it connected to the hotel’s Wi-Fi.

The scheme came to light after a recipient of the phishing emails contacted the hotel because its IP address appeared in information linked to the messages. Hotel staff found the computer and reported the matter to police.

The seized computer contained around 2.4 million email addresses and records of approximately 480,000 emails sent. The messages posed as communications from credit card companies and directed recipients to fake websites that captured their card details and other personal information. Investigators believe another person controlled the computer remotely and sent the emails through the hotel’s internet connection.

The case is not the first reported abuse of hotel internet infrastructure. In July 2026, Hackread.com reported on attackers who compromised hotel Wi-Fi gateways to redirect users to fake Microsoft 365 login pages. In the Kobe case, however, the alleged method involved hiding a computer on the network rather than hacking into the hotel’s Wi-Fi equipment.

Police Probe Other Suspected Fraud

The phishing investigation is not the only case involving the couple. In January 2026, Ye and Shen allegedly used a smartphone containing another person’s credit card details to buy three items, including down jackets, worth about 470,000 yen (approximately HK$24,000) at a commercial facility in Kobe.

Japanese media reported that police also recovered 74 smartphones from their home. Further investigation revealed that the couple had been using other people’s card details to make purchases since around 2024, with the total value amounting to 10 million yen. Police are examining the confiscated phones to identify the source of the card information and whether others were affected.

The couple was indicted in September 2026 in a separate case involving phishing emails sent through another Kobe hotel’s Wi-Fi and purchases made with other people’s card details. Police are investigating whether other people directed the activity or helped run the operation.

The couple’s response to the latest allegations has not been made public. The case does not necessarily indicate a weakness in the hotel’s Wi-Fi security. Investigators believe the computer was physically hidden in a guest room and left connected to the hotel’s network for remote use.

Dr. Aleksandr Yampolskiy, Co-Founder and CEO at SecurityScorecard, said the case highlights how criminals can exploit a business’s internet connection without necessarily breaching its systems. He shared the following comments with Hackread.com:

“What makes this case unusual is that the suspects allegedly brought their own equipment into a legitimate business rather than compromising its systems. By hiding a computer in a hotel room and controlling it remotely, the operators could use the hotel’s internet connection to send phishing emails without being physically present.

“Using a legitimate network does not automatically make phishing emails harder for security tools to detect, but it can make the people behind the operation more difficult to trace. Investigators following the network activity may initially be led to the hotel rather than the individuals controlling the device.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Scammers Abuse Frame.io Notifications to Steal Microsoft 365 Credentials
item.description:
Ocean Security found a phishing campaign, dubbed Phantom Preview, that abused legitimate Frame.io notifications and hidden PDF links to deliver fake Microsoft 365 login pages.

Cybersecurity researchers at Ocean Security identified a targeted adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing campaign on August 27, 2026, that abused Adobe Frame.io‘s legitimate share notifications to evade conventional email security checks.

Dubbed Phantom Preview, the campaign used a PDF to conceal a link to a fake Microsoft 365 login page that sent 22 emails to a single enterprise tenant within two hours. The messages came from the legitimate address [email protected] using the subject line “Jason Pitts shared ‘BTF Project’ with you,” making them appear to be routine file-sharing notifications.

The initial link led to Frame.io‘s genuine platform, where the shared PDF appeared as a non-clickable preview. The research, shared with Hackread.com, explains that this prevented the scanners investigating the share page from readily identifying the malicious destination hidden inside the original document.

An employee reported the first suspicious email just three minutes after it arrived, but conventional security checks had not flagged the threat.

AI Agent Traced the Hidden Link

Ocean Security used its AI investigation agent, Ray, to retrieve the original PDF through Frame.io‘s GraphQL GetAssetForDownload path. The agent examined the document’s /URI annotations, which specify link destinations, and uncovered a URL concealed behind the preview.

Ray also searched the tenant’s email history using the campaign’s subject line, identifying 21 other matching messages.

The link hidden inside the PDF redirected targets through a Cloudflare Pages subdomain using a 301 redirect. It then sent victims to a newly registered domain, msauth.biz. It was registered via eNom on August 6, 2026, and hosted on DigitalOcean.

When researchers checked it, VirusTotal showed zero detections across 91 security engines. This means the domain had not been flagged by any of those engines at the time.

The site used a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA to make it harder for security tools to check the page automatically. After a visitor passed the test, JavaScript created a URL containing a unique token, such as ?s=gQpS40I, that led to a fake Microsoft 365 login page.

According to Ocean Security, the token was designed to prevent the link from being easily shared or reused. This helped the attackers keep the phishing page tied to its intended victim.

Defending Against Trusted Share Notifications

Ocean Security has confirmed that Frame.io itself was not compromised. The attackers used its legitimate sharing system to send phishing emails that looked like normal file notifications.

Researchers recommend checking the files behind these notifications, not just the email sender or the link. In particular, security teams should check PDFs for hidden links to unfamiliar websites, including newly registered domains and suspicious Cloudflare Pages addresses.

An employee reported the first suspicious email just three minutes after it arrived, but conventional security checks had not flagged the threat.

AI Agent Traced the Hidden Link

Ocean Security used its AI investigation agent, Ray, to retrieve the original PDF through Frame.io‘s GraphQL GetAssetForDownload path. The agent examined the document’s /URI annotations, which specify link destinations, and uncovered a URL concealed behind the preview.

Ray also searched the tenant’s email history using the campaign’s subject line, identifying 21 other matching messages.

The link hidden inside the PDF redirected targets through a Cloudflare Pages subdomain using a 301 redirect. It then sent victims to a newly registered domain, msauth.biz. It was registered via eNom on August 6, 2026, and hosted on DigitalOcean.

When researchers checked it, VirusTotal showed zero detections across 91 security engines. This means the domain had not been flagged by any of those engines at the time.

The site used a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA to make it harder for security tools to check the page automatically. After a visitor passed the test, JavaScript created a URL containing a unique token, such as ?s=gQpS40I, that led to a fake Microsoft 365 login page.

According to Ocean Security, the token was designed to prevent the link from being easily shared or reused. This helped the attackers keep the phishing page tied to its intended victim.

Defending Against Trusted Share Notifications

Ocean Security has confirmed that Frame.io itself was not compromised. The attackers used its legitimate sharing system to send phishing emails that looked like normal file notifications.

Researchers recommend checking the files behind these notifications, not just the email sender or the link. In particular, security teams should check PDFs for hidden links to unfamiliar websites, including newly registered domains and suspicious Cloudflare Pages addresses.

item.title: BAE Systems Cyber Incident Disrupts US Bankruptcy Notices
item.description:
A cyber incident affecting BAE Systems halted US bankruptcy notices, forcing federal courts to change service procedures and adjust some deadlines.

A cybersecurity incident affecting systems operated by BAE Systems Inc. has halted the production and distribution of official notices for US bankruptcy cases. The nationwide outage began on October 9, 2026, disrupting paper and electronic notices sent to creditors, debtors and other parties.

The Administrative Office of the US Courts confirmed the incident on October 15. BAE Systems Inc., the US subsidiary of British defence company BAE Systems plc, operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) systems and websites on behalf of the federal judiciary.

Bankruptcy Notice Websites Offline

The outage has taken several websites offline, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov and notices.uscourts.gov. The National Creditor Registration Service is also unavailable.

“As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time,” the US Courts said.

Federal bankruptcy courts continue to accept filings and process cases, but the outage has stopped paper notices and electronic notices normally distributed through the BNC. Electronic notifications sent directly to registered CM/ECF users remain available in at least some districts, according to an update from the Eastern District of Tennessee.

The outage is also preventing some CM/ECF users from generating or printing creditor lists, sometimes called mailing matrices. Parties who depend on BNC delivery may therefore receive delayed information about hearings, court orders and case filings.

Courts Change Notice Procedures and Deadlines

Because bankruptcy courts administer their own local procedures, responses have varied by district.

Courts have introduced different measures to manage the disruption. In the Southern District of Florida, an order issued on October 16 requires trustees, debtors and their lawyers to handle certain notices normally sent through the BNC. The Eastern District of Louisiana has also assigned responsibility for mailing specified notices to debtors and trustees in certain cases filed since October 7.

Other courts have addressed proceedings affected by missing notices. The Southern District of Indiana and the Middle District of Pennsylvania directed that creditor meetings be adjourned, not concluded, when the outage prevents proper notice from being delivered.

The Southern District of Texas is allowing parties to request deadline extensions, with relief decided individually. Most courts have not introduced automatic deadline extensions, although the Middle District of Florida extended certain service deadlines, while the Eastern District of Texas granted a 30-day extension of the automatic stay in qualifying cases.

BAE Systems Investigating Incident

BAE Systems Inc. said the security incident was isolated to the BNC system and that no other company systems were affected. The company is working with the Administrative Office of the US Courts to restore the affected services.

Neither organisation has disclosed the cause, identified an attacker or said whether bankruptcy data was accessed or stolen. No restoration date had been announced at the time of writing.

Experts Warn of Risks From Reliance on Third-Party Systems

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, shared his comments with Hackread.com, saying the incident highlights how closely business and government processes are connected.

“A lot of people still think about computer security in terms of a DMZ. There’s an internal network to protect and an outside world to protect it from. But look at any modern large organization. They have multiple SaaS platforms, third-party integrations, and customer data flowing in and out of systems they don’t own or control. That perimeter is a lot messier than people want to believe.”

“I still don’t think the industry has caught up with the risks we introduced through cloud computing and SaaS. Now we’re adding AI to the mix, giving attackers new ways to target those services and exploit the connections between them. We weren’t caught up before. We’re certainly not ready now,” Strand added.

Jacob Krell, Senior Director of Secure AI Solutions and Cybersecurity at Suzu Labs, also shared his comments with Hackread.com, describing bankruptcy notices as “the machinery of due process” and pointing to the judiciary’s reliance on one contractor.

“Judges are already compensating, extending deadlines and continuing hearings district by district. That is the detail that should worry anyone procuring for the courts. The outage never touched a courtroom, yet it rewrote the calendar of every bankruptcy case in the country, because a vendor bought like routine IT has become load-bearing infrastructure for the justice system.”

“Restoring service is the urgent job. The standing question is why the noticing architecture has no alternate path, and I would want the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to write continuity requirements into the next BAE contract as strict as the ones the courts impose on themselves,” explained Krell.
